```{r library}
library(cdzoo)
has_pcalg <- requireNamespace("pcalg", quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
set.seed(20260902)
```

## Why

An analyst holding a published correlation matrix, or a table of pairwise
co-occurrence counts, but none of the original rows, asks a narrower version
of the same trust question: *I never had a data matrix to begin with -- can
I still get a structure, and can the recommender still tell me how much to
trust its routing when it never saw a single observation?* `cdzoo` treats a
sufficient statistic as a first-class input rather than a special case: it
can be discovered from directly, or handed to the recommender, which
routes it on the one characteristic a correlation matrix actually carries
and says plainly which of its usual diagnostics it could not run.

## What

`cd_correlation_from_counts()` assembles a correlation matrix from pairwise
two-by-two count tables, repairing it to the nearest valid correlation
matrix when the pairwise assembly is not itself positive-definite.
`cd_suffstat()` wraps a correlation matrix and its sample size as the
aggregated input `cd_auto()` recognises. `cd_discover_suffstat()` runs
constraint-based discovery directly on `(C, n)`: `method = "ggm"` needs no
back-end and returns the partial-correlation skeleton, `"pc"` and `"fci"`
add orientation through `pcalg`, and a `test` of `"gauss"` (significance) or
`"magnitude"` (effect size) decides how an edge is pruned. `cd_auto()` on a
`cd_suffstat` routes among the sufficient-statistic methods on the one
signature a correlation matrix carries -- a hint of latent structure -- and
`cd_explain()` states plainly which of the usual diagnostics an aggregated
input cannot support.

## Do

```{r graph-layout-helpers, include = FALSE}
# shared plotting helpers for the recovered-vs-truth figure below: lay the
# variables out on a circle, then read cd_edges() into segment coordinates.
.node_xy <- function(nm) {
  p1 <- length(nm)
  ang <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = p1 + 1L)[seq_len(p1)]
  data.frame(node = nm, x = cos(ang), y = sin(ang), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

.edge_segments <- function(amat, panel) {
  ed <- cd_edges(amat)
  xy <- .node_xy(colnames(amat))
  rownames(xy) <- xy$node
  ed$x0 <- xy[ed$from, "x"]
  ed$y0 <- xy[ed$from, "y"]
  ed$x1 <- xy[ed$to, "x"]
  ed$y1 <- xy[ed$to, "y"]
  ed$panel <- panel
  ed
}
```

### From counts to a correlation matrix

Co-occurrence data is often published as pairwise two-by-two tables: for
each pair of binary variables, the counts of both present, one present, or
neither.

```{r counts}
pairs <- data.frame(
  var_i = c("a", "a", "b"),
  var_j = c("b", "c", "c"),
  n11 = c(900, 110, 105),
  n10 = c(100, 890, 895),
  n01 = c(100, 90, 95),
  n00 = c(8900, 8910, 8905)
)
mat_c <- cd_correlation_from_counts(pairs, type = "phi")
repair <- attr(mat_c, "repair")
```

```{r counts-kable, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  round(mat_c, 3L),
  caption = "The phi-coefficient correlation matrix assembled from counts."
)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    diagnostic = c(
      "smallest eigenvalue, before repair", "smallest eigenvalue, after",
      "distortion (Frobenius norm of the change)"
    ),
    value = round(unlist(repair[c("eig_min_raw", "eig_min", "distortion")]), 4L)
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "The nearest-positive-definite repair the assembly needed."
)
```

The distortion is `r round(repair$distortion, 4L)`: the pairwise assembly
above was already a valid correlation matrix, so the repair step changed
nothing. A less internally consistent set of pairwise counts -- three
two-by-two tables whose implied correlations cannot all hold between three
variables at once -- would need a real repair, and the distortion would say
how much the reported matrix had to move to become one.

### Discovery directly from the statistic

```{r discover-suffstat}
res_ggm <- cd_discover_suffstat(mat_c, n = 10000, method = "ggm")
edges_ggm <- cd_edges(res_ggm)
edges_ggm
```

```{r discover-suffstat-kable, echo = FALSE}
# pandoc's smart-dash rendering turns the raw "-->"/"---" edge codes into
# unicode dashes inside an HTML table; relabel for display only.
edges_ggm_display <- edges_ggm
edges_ggm_display$type <- ifelse(
  edges_ggm_display$type == "-->", "directed", "undirected"
)
knitr::kable(
  edges_ggm_display,
  caption = paste0(
    "Edges recovered by the partial-correlation skeleton (no back-end ",
    "needed)."
  )
)
```

`method = "ggm"` needs nothing beyond base R: it thresholds partial
correlations directly, which is why this call runs regardless of what is
installed on the machine.

### Two ways to prune, at a sample size large enough to matter

At population-scale sample sizes, a significance-based test rejects
independence for almost every pair, so the graph saturates; the magnitude
test prunes by effect size instead, which is the behaviour a very large `n`
calls for.

```{r magnitude, eval = has_pcalg}
sim <- cd_scenario("linear_gaussian", seed = 1L)
mat_big <- stats::cor(sim$data)
gauss <- cd_discover_suffstat(mat_big, n = 5e6, method = "pc", test = "gauss")
magnitude <- cd_discover_suffstat(
  mat_big, n = 5e6, method = "pc", test = "magnitude"
)
edges_gauss <- cd_edges(gauss)
edges_magnitude <- cd_edges(magnitude)
score_magnitude <- cd_score(magnitude, sim$truth)
```

```{r magnitude-kable, echo = FALSE, eval = has_pcalg}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    test = c("gauss (significance)", "magnitude (effect size)"),
    edges = c(nrow(edges_gauss), nrow(edges_magnitude))
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0(
    "Edges recovered from the same correlation matrix at n = 5,000,000, ",
    "by pruning rule; the underlying scenario's true graph carries ",
    nrow(cd_edges(sim$truth)), " edges."
  )
)
```

```{r magnitude-skip, eval = !has_pcalg, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("pcalg is not installed on this build, so the significance-versus-",
    "magnitude comparison above is skipped.\n")
```

The magnitude test's graph is worth seeing beside the truth it is scored
against, which the edge table above cannot show on its own -- it lists
edges, not which ones point the way the truth does:

```{r fig-graph-vs-truth, eval = has_pcalg && has_ggplot2, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "The graph recovered from the correlation matrix alone (PC, magnitude-pruned, n = 5,000,000) beside the scenario's known truth. Both panels share the same variable layout; an arrow marks a directed edge, a plain line an edge whose direction was not resolved."}
edges_fig <- rbind(
  .edge_segments(magnitude@graph, "recovered (PC, magnitude test)"),
  .edge_segments(sim$truth, "known truth")
)
edges_fig$kind <- factor(
  ifelse(edges_fig$type == "-->", "directed", "undirected"),
  levels = c("directed", "undirected")
)
nodes_fig <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    .node_xy(colnames(sim$truth)), panel = "recovered (PC, magnitude test)"
  ),
  data.frame(.node_xy(colnames(sim$truth)), panel = "known truth")
)

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = edges_fig[edges_fig$kind == "undirected", ],
    ggplot2::aes(x = x0, y = y0, xend = x1, yend = y1, colour = kind),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = edges_fig[edges_fig$kind == "directed", ],
    ggplot2::aes(x = x0, y = y0, xend = x1, yend = y1, colour = kind),
    linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(2.2, "mm"), type = "closed")
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = nodes_fig, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y), size = 9, shape = 21,
    fill = "white", colour = "grey30", stroke = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = nodes_fig, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, label = node), size = 3.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_d(
    name = "edge", option = "D", end = 0.7, drop = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel) +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1.3, 1.3), ylim = c(-1.3, 1.3)) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank()
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Recovered structure against the known truth")
```

```{r fig-graph-vs-truth-skip, eval = !(has_pcalg && has_ggplot2), echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("The recovered-versus-truth figure needs pcalg and ggplot2 both",
    "installed; it is skipped when either is absent.\n")
```

```{r score-kable, echo = FALSE, eval = has_pcalg}
knitr::kable(
  score_magnitude, digits = 3,
  caption = "The magnitude-pruned graph, scored against the known truth."
)
```

### Letting the recommender route it

Wrapping the statistic as `cd_suffstat()` lets `cd_auto()` recommend a
method over it:

```{r auto, eval = has_pcalg}
ss <- cd_suffstat(mat_big, n = nrow(sim$data))
rec_ss <- cd_auto(ss)
cd_explain(rec_ss)
```

```{r auto-skip, eval = !has_pcalg, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("pcalg is not installed on this build, so the sufficient-statistic",
    "recommendation above is skipped.\n")
```

### Passing the result on

A recovered graph carries its provenance into the canonical
`orchestra_manifest` exactly as a data-driven result does
(`inferential_target = "structure"`, the token this package's enrolment
added to the contract), so an aggregated-input discovery is verifiable
downstream just like any other member's:

```{r manifest, eval = has_pcalg}
manifest_ss <- as_orchestra_manifest(rec_ss, seed = 1L)
manifest_ss@inferential_target
verify_manifest(manifest_ss)$ok
```

```{r manifest-skip, eval = !has_pcalg, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("pcalg is not installed on this build, so the manifest example above",
    "is skipped.\n")
```

The whole path -- counts to a correlation matrix, discovery from the
statistic, a routed recommendation, and a verifiable manifest -- runs
without ever holding a row-level data set.

## Read

```{r read-text, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (has_pcalg) {
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0(
      "Yes: a correlation matrix is enough to get a structure, and the ",
      "recommender states plainly what it could not check to get there. ",
      "The magnitude-pruned graph recovers the true skeleton exactly ",
      "(skeleton F1 = %.0f) but its structural Hamming distance is %d, ",
      "not zero, because %d of its seven edges point the wrong way or ",
      "were left unresolved; a correlation matrix alone under-determines ",
      "orientation the way a full data matrix would not, and the figure ",
      "shows exactly which edges that cost fell on. The recommender's ",
      "own rationale above states the same limit in words before any ",
      "graph is drawn: it names the one signature a correlation matrix ",
      "carries -- a hint of latent structure from the matrix's condition ",
      "number -- and says outright that the non-Gaussianity, ",
      "nonlinearity, and equal-variance tests the data-driven route ",
      "leans on need row-level data it does not have.\n"
    ),
    score_magnitude$skeleton_f1,
    score_magnitude$shd,
    score_magnitude$shd
  ))
} else {
  cat(
    "pcalg is not installed on this build, so the comparison this section",
    "reads from did not run; the sections marked skipped above state",
    "what was missing.\n"
  )
}
```

## Limits

The recommender's route over a sufficient statistic is coarser than its
route over row-level data by construction, not by an oversight this
vignette works around: a correlation matrix carries no information about
non-Gaussianity, nonlinear mechanisms, or unequal residual variances, so
none of those signatures can fire, and every sufficient-statistic
recommendation reports lower confidence for exactly that reason. The
repair step in `cd_correlation_from_counts()` finds the nearest valid
correlation matrix to an internally inconsistent set of pairwise counts; it
does not, and cannot, recover which of the original counts was wrong, only
how far the assembled matrix had to move to become coherent. The
significance-versus-magnitude contrast above is a property of the test, not
of the sample size on its own: a smaller `n` would not saturate the
significance test the way `n = 5,000,000` does here, and a data set whose
true effect sizes are themselves small would still saturate a
magnitude-pruned graph toward the empty one. None of this vignette's
examples carries an unmeasured confounder deliberately; a latent-structure
hint from a near-singular correlation routes to a confounder-robust method,
but this vignette does not construct a case where that route actually
fires.

## What to read next

*A benchmark harness and recommender for causal discovery* covers the
ordinary case this vignette does not: a row-level data matrix, the full set
of routing signatures, consensus across several methods, and the benchmark
evidence the routing is grounded in.

## Reproduce

`set.seed(20260902)` guards the top-level session; the simulated scenario
this vignette's correlation matrix is drawn from is additionally seeded
explicitly through `cd_scenario()`'s own `seed = 1L` argument, so the same
call reproduces the same matrix regardless of what ran before it in the
session.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
